idiom_name: persisted request + distinct-principal check in the server-side authorization middleware
implementation_notes: Node/JavaScript has no role or principal machinery of its own: identity arrives with the verified session or token and the duty split must be enforced server-side, in the middleware or service that performs the decisive step. What replaces the classic structure is the persisted request (initiatedBy plus its revision) and a check comparing the acting principal's stable id with it - never a client-supplied field. node:permissions can fence what the process may touch, but the Node documentation is explicit that the permission model is a 'seat belt' and does not protect against malicious code, so it is not the separation mechanism; the second pair of eyes is either a different authenticated human acting through the API or, structurally, a different process or service with its own credentials. Hiding the button or shipping a role claim the client can read is presentation, not enforcement.
pitfalls: One Node process holds every duty in memory: when maker and checker routes share a trust domain the split is a policy convention, so use separate services or credentials where the boundary must survive a compromised component.
Identity taken from the request body, query string or a client-decoded JWT claim can be spoofed; the principal must come from the verified session/token on the server.
Asynchronous handlers invite read-compare-write races; the distinctness condition belongs in the same atomic write (conditional UPDATE with a row-count check) as the state transition.
